fiordland_crested_penguin.title: THE PENGUIN THAT NESTS IN A RAINFOREST
fiordland_crested_penguin.script: Meet the Fiordland crested penguin, called tawaki in New Zealand. Unlike the penguins most people picture on open ice, tawaki raise chicks in dense coastal rainforest. Their yellow eyebrow feathers are unmistakable, but hidden burrows make them hard to count. Researchers have mapped more than a thousand nests, suggesting the population may be larger than earlier estimates. After breeding, the birds travel thousands of miles to feed before replacing their feathers. The twist is that scientists are still discovering how this secretive jungle penguin survives.

red_fox_mousing.title: WHY FOXES DIVE HEADFIRST INTO THE GROUND
red_fox_mousing.script: A red fox sometimes jumps high and lands nose-first in grass or snow. It looks like a mistake, but the fox is hunting. Its ears pick up tiny movements of rodents hidden under cover. After listening and adjusting its position, the fox leaps to pin down its prey. That move is called mousing. Young foxes practice quick turns and pounces while playing. Adults may hide extra food to eat later. When a fox seems to be doing a dramatic faceplant, it is not clumsy. It is calculating dinner. It listens first, then launches the jump at just the right moment, turning ordinary grass into a hidden hunting ground.
red_fox_mousing.caption: A fox faceplant is a hunting move. 🦊 #RedFox #FoxFacts #WildVox

bald_eagle_aerial_survival.title: WHY A BALD EAGLE GETS CHASED BY SMALLER BIRDS
bald_eagle_aerial_survival.script: A bald eagle is a powerful predator, but smaller birds can chase it away. Ravens sometimes mob eagles near nesting or feeding areas. The eagle's broad wings are built for efficient soaring, not for winning every aerial argument. It scans water for fish, grabs food with curved talons, and sometimes scavenges. Young bald eagles lack the famous white head and tail. They gain adult plumage over several years. Even a top predator must choose its battles, and sometimes the smallest bird wins the airspace.
bald_eagle_aerial_survival.caption: Even bald eagles get chased by smaller birds. 🦅 #BaldEagle #BirdFacts #WildVox

sea_otter_kelp_guardian.title: THE FURRY PREDATOR THAT PROTECTS KELP FORESTS
sea_otter_kelp_guardian.script: A sea otter looks like a floating teddy bear, but this little predator helps protect an entire underwater forest. Sea otters eat sea urchins. Without enough otters, urchins can multiply and chew through kelp forests, leaving barren seafloors. With otters around, kelp has a better chance to recover, sheltering fish and other ocean life. Some otters even use rocks to crack open shellfish. And unlike seals, they rely on incredibly dense fur to stay warm. The surprise? One fluffy sea otter can help an entire kelp forest thrive.
sea_otter_kelp_guardian.caption: Sea otters protect kelp forests. 🦦🌊 #SeaOtter #KelpForest #WildVox

african_bush_elephant_bee_alarm.title: WHY ELEPHANTS WARN EACH OTHER ABOUT BEES
african_bush_elephant_bee_alarm.script: Even the world's largest land animal can be scared away by something tiny: bees. African bush elephants have sensitive skin around their eyes and trunks, so stings are a real threat. Researchers found that elephants react to buzzing and make special alarm calls that warn the herd. Families can then move away together. Elephants use deep rumbles and touch to communicate, and experienced adults help protect calves. Scientists have even tested beehive fences to discourage elephants from entering farms. Imagine being a giant, and your biggest warning sound comes from a buzzing bee.
african_bush_elephant_bee_alarm.caption: Even elephants respect angry bees. 🐘🐝 #AfricanElephant #WildVox
